 Through that lens, it’s easy to see why big companies are protecting other big companies. People finally found a thing to do with AI tools that gives consumers a bit more control over the devices they bought; it must be immediately stamped out.

“This vibe-code hacking is only called ‘reverse’ when somebody who lacks a trillion dollars is doing it,” the science fiction author Bruce Sterling tweeted. “When you ‘reverse engineer’ the entire Internet Common Crawl, you just built a nice AI model.”

items.title: Dad Asked 6-Year-Old Daughter if ‘She Had the Gun’ Before He Left Her in Line for Pokémon Cards
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Pokémon released its Mega Evolution Delta Region cards this week and one man in Charleston, South Carolina wanted them so badly that he left his 6-year-old daughter in line at Target at 1 am with a pillow and a blanket. 

According to the incident report obtained by 404 Media, the person next to the little girl in line heard the father ask if his daughter “had the gun” before he left her alone at Target for more than an hour. Later, the father he left his daughter behind so “he could maintain his place in line and avoid missing the opportunity to purchase the cards.”

Pokémon cards are and people will wait to go to wild lengths to secure them. Waiting in line outside of a store for days before a new release is routine. John-Michael Dooley was waiting in line outside of a Target in Charleston, South Carolina with his 6-year-old daughter on the morning of November 6 when he decided to run home. He didn’t want to lose his place in line so he left his daughter behind “sleeping on the concrete,” according to a record of 911 calls obtained by 404 Media.

Other people waiting for Pokémon cards watched Dooley drive away and called the cops when he didn’t return. One guy on the scene started a timer on his phone when Dooley left and called the cops once it hit 45 minutes. “[He] advised later that he continued the timer on his phone, and the point in which the father returned to target showed 1 hour and 6 minutes,” according to an incident report obtained by 404 Media.

The person in line next to the 6-year-old “recalled the father waking his daughter up before he left and advised her he was ‘taking the dogs home,’” the report said. “Following this, [he] recalled hearing the father ask the daughter if ‘she had the gun’ before leaving.’ All parties on scene advised that the offender did not ask anyone to care or look after his daughter, and all stated the offender simply left her there by herself.”

The cops woke the girl up and she told them “she was at Target in line to get Pokémon cards with her father when the store opened,” according to the incident report. The police didn’t find a gun. “The only items the juvenile had in her possession when she was located was a pillow and a green blanket.”

Dooley returned to the line to find police talking to his daughter. “The juvenile still was unsure to the whereabouts of her father at this time,” the report said. “Several minutes after this, I could hear and see a dark colored SUV driving in the parking lot of Target in our direction. As the vehicle got closer, the [person who called 911] yelled out ‘That`s him.’”

Dooley got out of his car and police arrested him. “The offender was brought back to my patrol vehicle at which point he continued to say that he had only left to bring his dogs home,” the report said. “The offender reiterated this several times while also confirming that he left his 6-year-old daughter unattended for a period of time.” Dooley has been charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.

Pokémon card collecting has been at the center of a few strange crimes over the past few years. Fights broke out in multiple Target parking lots earlier this year when a set dropped.

Last week, the UK imposed one of the strictest, most vague (and therefore overly broad) new laws around pornography in recent memory. Recording yourself having consensual kinky sex in private could come with jail time, as could watching other people do it. And sex workers are the ones to feel the repercussions of bad laws like these first, of course, with many reporting content disappearing from their online stores en masse. Keep reading to learn more about what it covers, and how creators are responding.

“I adore breath play. I love being strangled, suffocated and drowned, and I love strangling and suffocating others. Waterboarding: that’s my favourite,” Melissa Todd, a UK-based writer and sex worker, told me. “Many women do: it really isn’t only horrid men forcing us to do these dreadful depraved acts. Interrupting oxygen supply produces the most intense sensation of euphoria. I enjoy it in my private life, and I offer it in sessions too.”

she and anyone else in the UK distributing or possessing certain types of choking, suffocation, breath play, strangulation and a bunch of other types of porn — even if it’s just recorded in the privacy of their homes and not for sale on a porn site — could face up to five years in prison. 

This is, predictably, already a huge mess for sex workers. Adult creators watched platforms remove hundreds of their videos — even when the creators thought they were in compliance with the law. These creators say they were blindsided by the removals, since the content didn’t seem to violate the law at all. Creators are reporting one platform in particular, Clips4Sale, is purging content with little notice, “a precautionary measure,” with videos disappearing in the hundreds.

“Of course, we were all aware of the new Act coming in and prepared accordingly, but not for anything at this scale. We've had nothing since and they've been tweeting as normal,” adult creator Sophia Truee said. Clips4Sale launched in 2003 and caters heavily to fetish content. “It's a huge blow to this area of the industry, and I can only hope things will be communicated soon. We, as creators, understand how difficult it is to be a content site in this current climate, but communication has not been prioritized,” Truee said, noting that this is happening right before the holidays, with Black Friday being one of the most popular times for creators selling content. “For many, this will be devastating, as over 20 years of the work will have just been wiped.”

items.title: How Earth Lost a Billion Years of Its History
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that drew a blank, felt the squeeze, played the queen, and made donkey-bull love.

First, scientists shed new light on how Earth ended up losing more than a billion years of its geological record, a puzzle that has resisted explanation for decades. Then: octopuses in tight spots, a topless spear-brandishing Celt, and a tale of unlikely tail.

“Blank Space” (Earth’s Version)

Earth doesn’t trouble itself too much with keeping intact archives. With its tectonic activity and erosive forces, our planet is constantly wiping out huge chunks of its own memory, creating gaps in the geological record called unconformities. 

The Great Unconformity, the largest gap of this kind, reveals that Earth straight-up deleted more than a billion years of strata, for reasons that remain hotly debated and mysterious. Sandstone that dates back to the Cambrian period some 538 million years is often found directly on top of ancient “basement” rocks that date back anywhere from 1.2 billion to 1.8 billion years ago. This missing layer shows up around the world, hinting that it was erased by a global event.  

Now, scientists have placed the origins of the Great Unconformity deep inside Earth’s mantle, during the tectonic tumult of supercontinent breakup.

“The cause or causes of the Great Unconformity are unknown,” said authors Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong. “The proposed mechanisms include extensive glacial erosion during Snowball Earth (about 720–635 million years ago), rifting and plume activity, sea-level fall and mantle-driven dynamic topography.” 

“These processes have not been dynamically tested, with limited comparison between global models and global datasets to explain the spatial distribution of the Great Unconformity,” the team added. 

To fill the knowledge gap about the geological gap, the researchers ran models of the formation and breakup of ancient supercontinents during the eons preceding the Cambrian period, when complex life rapidly proliferated in Earth’s seas. Massive landmasses were pushed upward by motions in Earth’s mantle during this time. Exposed to erosive forces such as weather, glaciers, and eventually oceans, they became sanded down over time, creating the vast void. 

“Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes,” the team concluded.

Scientists will no doubt continue to of this planet-wide memory lapse, but there is consensus that the same mechanisms also set the stage for the emergence of complex life during the Cambrian. No matter what caused the Great Unconformity, we partly owe our existence to it today. 

Putting the squeeze on octopuses   

We’ll move now from massive gaps in Earth’s memory to tiny gaps that octopuses can somehow squeeze through. These tentacled escape artists can famously maneuver their way through passages that seem impossibly small relative to their bodies, an ability that has spawned a subgenre of viral videos.

Now, scientists have discovered the secrets of “octopus-squeezing behavior” by observing two species—the common octopus () and the Mayan octopus ()—navigating small holes in laboratory containers. 

“Our study demonstrates that octopuses employ two primary strategies, 3-step and 4-step, for squeezing through narrow spaces,” said researchers led by Wenci Xin of the National University of Singapore. “The key distinction between these strategies lies in whether the body is squeezed separately from the arms.” 

The first two steps were probing the aperture and then shifting a few arms through it. Navigating the tightest spaces required breaking up the final passage into two parts: Pulling the remaining arms to the other side, and then compressing the mantle behind the head so they could fit through last.

In addition to documenting these amazing feats of flexibility in nature, the study is the perfect excuse to revisit the classic episode “Squeeze.”

When Rome invaded Britain 2,000 years ago, they had the help of an inside man—or was it an inside ? In a new article, an archaeologist makes the case that the British king Verica, who aided the Roman invasion of their own homeland, was actually a queen that has been misgendered lo these many centuries. 

Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica was a woman based in part on the leader’s Latin name, which ends in the suffix “a” which is common for women, as opposed to names ending in “-us” for men. 

Coins also depict Verica using “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female in contrast to the overtly masculine warriors on the issues of Iron Age rulers like Tasciovanus and Caratacus,” according to Russell. 

Women leaders weren’t unheard of in Celtic Britain, as evidenced by the queens Cartimandua and Boudica, who lived in the same century as Verica. Regardless of whether Verica was among their ranks, this leader was a consequential figure in the Roman takeover of Britain. 

Achille and Patroclo: More than friends  

Scientists who were conducting fieldwork on monkeys in Ethiopia serendipitously stumbled upon a very different discovery—a tender same-sex relationship between a bull and a donkey.

Achille, a bull, and Patroclo, a donkey, belong to different owners, but they graze together by day. Despite the availability of other males and females in their pasture, this pair has developed a strong socio-sexual bond that includes nuzzling, licking, and Achille sexually mounting Patroclo.

“Patroclo frequently presented his hindquarters toward Achille and nipped him,” said  researchers led by André Beirão da Cruz of the University of Pisa. “In the only two instances in which Achille approached and mounted another male donkey, this individual showed clear avoidance behaviours and displayed threatening facial expressions (e.g. ear flattening), which were never observed in Patroclo during the 51 mountings (34 with intromission) with Achille.”

Same-sex sexual behavior is extremely common in nature and has a wide variety of possible explanations, including social cohesion, mistaken identity, or lack of access to opposite-sex mates. But what Achille and Patroclo have is special. Despite being different species and having alternate mating options, the pair share a highly selective and reciprocal social and sexual bond. 

“Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship” and “the strength of the animals’ social bond,” the team concluded.

In addition to this heartwarming tale, the study goes to show that you never know what you might find when you chase your goals. The researchers were there to watch geladas, but it turned out those primates weren’t the only animals monkeying around.

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss election outcomes and code as a human endeavor.

This week I got a real wave of ‘oh man this fucking sucks’ regarding AI. I won’t link to it because it’s just a rando person, but scrolling Reddit I saw someone who said they used Claude to build stuff with Max. Max, or Max/MSP, is a visual programming language that is heavily used in the world of music and visual art. It is the foundation of a lot of electronic music. You can build essentially anything in it, if you put in the work to understand how to put it together. And that can be a lot of work.

I’ve built various little things in Max. I made a tool that takes a drum break and generates new, random drum and bass style breaks from it. I am a big, big fan of generative music (both listening and making) where you create rules and parameters, press play, and let the rules decide what comes out. I made another that has various synthesizers, and from scratch manipulates the audio so they sound like Tibetan singing bowls, with their harmonies and individual melodies morphing over time. I also started working on the visual part of Max, called Jitter, to take audio output from Max and generate visuals.

These were deeply difficult to make, at least for me. I can code in Python, but this was of course learning an entirely new language, and one whose syntax (and everything really) is entirely different. It took lots of long nights of figuring out, okay, this device connects to this one, this thing goes here, okay, I’ve figured it out. 

Code is a human endeavor. It can be for a lot of people a creative pursuit (it was for me for a while). But Max coding is human. It is code to create music. And now here was someone using Claude to bypass all of that. To cheat themselves out of the satisfaction of learning an instrument, or in this case a new musical language. I have no idea if they understand what Claude made, or whether they care. But this one was a real gut punch to me.

Music creation is one of the areas I do not want AI to touch at all (at least unless it is some very specific use case with the artist’s own data, or something similar). For years as a musician, I simply would not use other peoples’ samples because it felt like a shortcut, it didn’t feel like mine (I know this is an extreme position, and I love lots of sample based music, I just don’t want to make it). This is now even further: you want AI to not only make the music (like Suno), but also the tools that can help you create it in the first place. I dunno man, it just fucking sucks.

I held a few articles I’ve written this week back for next week because the election became the story this week, and rightly so. The main thing I published this week was my analysis of the election, which lots of you have said you liked and which a lot of people suggested I must have had fun writing. I did have fun writing it, thank you v much, but I also had a great time this week consuming the memes, the livestreams, the podcasts. Great week for content. 

If you’ll remember, after Trump got elected a second time, we started to see a handful of people cancel their subscriptions with us not because they said they didn’t like our work, but because they didn’t see what the point was. They figured it was all over, that journalism was useless, that there was not much that could be done to stem fascism in the country. The last two years have been brutal, about as bad as I thought they could be and in many ways worse. A day or two after his election, we all cowrote a piece called “Why the Work Still Matters.” If I’m being honest, I think we wrote it in part because we were scared that people would just mass unsubscribe from us because they felt greater despair, and we wanted to maybe convince ourselves a bit that we could still do this work under Trump. 

I’m going to quote from that piece at length for a second: 

“We cannot and will not make false promises to you about the power of journalism—especially at a small publication—to stop the country’s knowing march into authoritarianism. But we can explain our approach to the work and we can demonstrate to you why it matters,” we wrote. “We cannot set the bar for our success at the systemic saving of democracy. Instead, we have found that our work can and does make incremental positive change at the local, state, and federal level, and that, over time, these small improvements become increasingly important.  

“Our work is populist in that we recognize that many of the problems plaguing the United States today and which are factors that have laid the groundwork for Trump’s return—income inequality, a lack of affordable housing, unstable work, the widespread inability to tell what is real and what is fake—are being at least partially driven by technology and/or the immense wealth of the people who own tech companies,” we added. “Most of our articles tell the stories of hyperspecific communities of people who are using technology or are impacted by it in some way. By focusing on how technology impacts people, we have found that we can impact technology and make the world slightly better, regardless of who the president is.”

There’s lots more there. This was published basically exactly two years ago. Since then we have seen many terrible things happen; you’ve read about them on our website and elsewhere. I am too tired at the moment to dig through our archives or rack my brain for more about the horrors of the last two years. But we have also seen, as we hoped but couldn’t know for sure, people organize to support each other, grassroots movements against AI-powered surveillance, ICE’s brutality, Silicon Valley’s excesses, AI data centers, inequality, and more. 

We know for a fact that a lot of our work has led directly to incremental progress over the last two years. I don’t propose that our blogs created the wave we saw Tuesday, but we’ve heard directly from people who said our reporting inspired them to, for example, get an anti-ALPR license plate regulation put on their town’s ballot. Their town overwhelmingly voted to ban the tech. There are so many things that everyone who has been working for a better future has done over the last two years (and long before that), that made these election results possible, and that made Tuesday feel so satisfying.

It’s like the coin pusher game at the arcade. You diligently put quarter after quarter in and maybe it feels like nothing happens. I leave the arcade and you put some quarters in. Every once in a while, a few quarters come out the bottom that make you feel like maybe the game isn’t as rigged as you think it is. Eventually, something like Tuesday happens and zillions of quarters come out. Maybe a few of our quarters helped out. I don’t know if that metaphor makes any sense whatsoever, but it feels like Tuesday was something of a dam bursting. I’ve heard it described as the collective exhale after a decade of misery that has created the space for progress. There is so much more work to be done!

One thing I am really excited to see come of this week is the wholesale rejection of data centers specifically. Matthew Gault wrote a great writeup of how this played out across the country, so I don’t want to repeat it too much. But in the last year or so, the explosion of data center projects (and yes, everyone’s calling them “compute campuses” now, which a bunch of overly online people noticed this week too — they’ve been pulling that shit for a while now, but I don’t think the phrase is actually any more palatable than “data center” anyway so, who cares) have bummed me massively. They’re a huge, destructive, ugly, extractive symbol of what the tech industry has become, but instead of remaining concentrated in Palo Alto or in an Apple Store as physically cursed places, they’re taking up miles of land around the country, sucking dry everything around them, returning nothing but bullshit. In 10 years these warehouses will stand abandoned by all stakeholders and we’ll all get nothing but shitty tap water in return. Combined with Flock’s presence around the country, they’ve infiltrated our physical spaces in ways that make Big Tech’s impact on our lives impossible to ignore.

And I wonder if that’s part of what we’re seeing in these election results. As Gault wrote: "These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for Local Progress, told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”

items.title: UK Sex Workers Wake Up to Sites Purging Their Content Following Porn Ban
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
Immediately after the of porn fantasies involving choking, breath-restriction, and relative roleplay, adult creators watched platforms remove hundreds of their videos — even when the creators thought they were in compliance with the law. These creators say they were blindsided by the removals, since the content didn’t seem to violate the law at all.

Creators are reporting one platform in particular, Clips4Sale, is purging content with little notice, “a precautionary measure.”   

Some creators who’ve contacted Clips4Sale to appeal these removals have shared screenshots online of the reply the platform sends: “At this time, we have implemented a general restriction on content availability in the UK to ensure compliance with applicable regulatory requirements,” Clips4Sale support replies, according to these screenshots, viewed by 404 Media. “This is a precautionary measure and does not necessarily indicate that your clips contain prohibited content or violate our policies. We are continuing to review affected content, and additional clips will be made available to UK buyers as they are reviewed and cleared.” 

Updates to the UK’s Crime and Policing Act went into force on Friday. The law criminalizes a list of sexual acts, including downloading or publishing choking and incest roleplay content. The law is vague and overbroad, criminalizing “strangulation or suffocation” and “certain types” of incest roleplay. There's a lot of confusion among sex workers and fans about what this encompasses, and seemingly could include various kinds of gagging, face sitting, and roleplay. Violating this law, either as someone in possession of noncompliant content or publishing it, carries a risk of up to five years in prison. 

UK-based creator Sophia Truee told me that Clips4Sale removed more than 75 percent of her content — 392 out of 506 videos — with the platform flagging it as requiring edits without noting what needed to change. Truee makes POV content where she’s alone talking to the camera. Many more creators have shared on social media that content that shouldn’t be in violation of the law has been caught in the crossfire on Clips4Sale specifically. 

In an email sent to creators on Thursday, the day before the law went into force, Clips4Sale said it would be reviewing “both the video content and its details, including titles, tags, keywords, and descriptions” of content that creators have uploaded to the site. It told creators no action was required. “Affected clips will be hidden automatically starting November 6. If you'd like to make a clip available in the UK again, you can edit the content or its details as needed and submit the changes for compliance review.” Approved content would go back up, the company said.

Another message from Clips4Sale on creators’ dashboards said: “As we gain further clarity on the regulatory requirements, we expect to be able to make additional content available again to UK users, wherever permitted. These restrictions apply only to the UK and will not affect your content's availability in other markets where it is permitted.” According to the law, however, if creators based in the UK possess that content, they’re still facing jail time.  

“Of course, we were all aware of the new Act coming in and prepared accordingly, but not for anything at this scale. We've had nothing since and they've been tweeting as normal,” Truee said. Clips4Sale launched in 2003 and caters heavily to fetish content. “It's a huge blow to this area of the industry, and I can only hope things will be communicated soon. We, as creators, understand how difficult it is to be a content site in this current climate, but communication has not been prioritized,” Truee said, noting that this is happening right before the holidays, with Black Friday being one of the most popular times for creators selling content. “For many, this will be devastating, as over 20 years of the work will have just been wiped.” 

Madame Caramel, another UK-based creator using Clips4Sale, that out of 900 clips she had available on the platform, she now has 198 left. Another creator, that the platform restricted 931 of her clips from UK audiences. “All of them [had] utterly NOTHING to do with the UK laws,” she wrote. There are many, many more creators across social media reporting that they’ve woken up to their clip sites gutted with no warning, even though their content wasn’t non-compliant by the letter of the law.

With the speed at which content has been purged en masse, and with some creators reporting instant rejections of content that should actually be compliant with the law, Clips4Sale may be auto-moderating with a very wide net, and sifting through reviews creators are now forced to send for legal content. This is something most social media platforms do to try to comply whenever over-broad laws or payment processor regulations hit. 

Other platforms are also attempting to comply now that the law is in effect. LoyalFans has a notice on its homepage for fans addressing the new law. It says: “These changes may also apply to content you've purchased, downloaded, or saved privately on your devices. Non-compliant content in your Loyalfans account will be removed on November 5, with no further action required from your side. We encourage you to understand the new law and review any affected content you have downloaded, or stored privately, whether on your phone, computer, or cloud storage.” 

LoyalFans updated its terms of use on Thursday to include strangulation or suffocation, in its unacceptable content list, “including any content, whether real or simulated, that explicitly and realistically depicts a person strangling or suffocating another person, such as applying pressure to the neck or obstructing the nose or mouth,” the terms now say. “This content is prohibited regardless of whether the participants consent, and even if it is fantasy-based, roleplay, or digitally created.” Several creators using LoyalFans have posted on social media saying they’ve had hundreds of videos removed from their accounts on that platform, too.

JustForFans, an LGBTQ and kink content site, posted on X earlier this week that creators should review their content and use its new “restrict this content” option to keep it from being viewed by users in the UK. The platform also said that it would be scanning every new video upload for consent requirements and content restrictions. “If we find content that should be restricted in the UK, we will restrict it and you can review it in a new section of your Media Center called Restricted Content. The page will tell you what we found and give you options right on that page to fix it: re-word a post, replace a video with another video, delete the video, or tell us we are wrong, and why you believe we are wrong. A staff member will review your changes,” it said. 

“The UK's new pornography restrictions are creating a lot of uncertainty for adult creators, and we want to give our models options rather than simply take away their work. We're reviewing new and old content for potentially restricted material, blocking flagged content from UK viewers and giving models the ability to correct or challenge those decisions. Creators can also restrict individual videos themselves or block access from the UK entirely," JustForFans founder Dominic Ford said in a statement. “The law is nuanced and not particularly well-adapted to gay content. The spirit of the law is about protecting women, but some things don't translate directly to gay culture. For example, 'daddy' is an archetype, not a claim that someone is your actual father, so we're not treating those scenes as automatically prohibited. Our priority is to comply with the law without unnecessarily restricting content elsewhere. We also want models in England and Wales to understand that the law covers possession, not just publication, so they need to take extra precautions.”

The vagueness of the law, combined with the use of auto-moderation on sites like Clips4Sale, have come together to create a nightmare for creators. “This highlights the lack of protection sex workers and content creators have when laws aren't properly researched and clearly written. We do our very best to stay compliant and ensure everyone's safety by following the rules,” Truee said. “This highlights the unprecedented use of AI in moderation and the lack of clear instructions from the government.” 

Clips4Sale told 404 Media in a statement: "The UK law carries criminal penalties for possessing or distributing consensual kink and fetish content made by consenting adults, meaning our creators risk arrest if we allow them to distribute banned content in the UK. Unfortunately, there’s no good guidance as to what content might or might not now be illegal. As a result, we’re being aggressive for the time being when it comes to limiting content. We know this is not what creators want, and it’s not what we want. Over the coming weeks, we hope to be able to clear clips that were limited during this precautionary period, after we’ve had a chance to review them more closely. This law is impacting an already marginalized community, mostly women, mostly queer or gender-nonconforming, heavily stigmatized and discriminated against. As with most sex censorship, the burden falls heavily on communities with the least amount of power. We will work with the UK government to comply with the law and our creators to keep them safe."

Updated Friday, November 6 1:03 p.m. EST with comment from Clips4Sale.
